# Automation Usage Decisions: Controlling Intent and Appraisal Errors in a Target Detection Task

**Hall P. Beck,** Appalachian State University, Boone, North Carolina, **Mary T. Dzindolet,** Cameron University, Lawton, Oklahoma, and **Linda G. Pierce,** Army Research Laboratory, Aberdeen, Maryland

**Background:** It was proposed that misuse and disuse often occur because operators (a) cannot determine if automation or a nonautomated alternative maximizes the likelihood of task success (appraisal errors) or (b) know the utilities of the options but disregard this information when deciding to use automation (intent errors). **Objective:** This investigation assessed the effectiveness of performance feedback, a procedure developed to attenuate appraisal errors, and scenario training, an intervention designed to decrease intent errors. **Methods:** Operators given feedback were told how many errors they and an automated device made on a target detection task. Scenario training took operators through the thought processes of optimal decision makers after the utilities of the automated and nonautomated alternatives had been determined. Following 200 training trials, participants chose between relying on their observations or an automated device. **Results:** There was little misuse, but disuse rates were high (84%) among operators receiving neither feedback nor scenario training. Operators paired with a more accurate machine and given feedback made approximately twice as many errors as the automated device. Nevertheless, intent errors were commonplace; 55% of the operators who received feedback without scenario training did not rely on automation. Feedback effectiveness was enhanced when used in conjunction with scenario training; the disuse rate decreased to 29%. **Conclusion:** A combination of feedback and scenario training was more effective in mitigating disuse than either intervention used in isolation. **Application:** An important application of these findings is that operator training programs should incorporate techniques to control intent and appraisal errors.

## INTRODUCTION

A shortcoming of many highly automated systems is that they are inflexible and limited in their capacities to respond to unanticipated events. To rectify this problem, human operators frequently are given the option of using or not using an automated device. For instance, a subway engineer may rely on automation to stop the train in good weather but switch to manual operation if the tracks are icy. In such situations the optimal decision is to employ the mode of control that maximizes safety. Disuse is underutilization of automation, failing to use automation that would improve the likelihood of a successful performance. Misuse is overreliance, using an automated device when the task could be better accomplished by a non-automated or less automated alternative (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997).

Empirical studies and accident analyses (e.g., Lee & See, 2004; National Transportation Safety Board, 1996) indicate that misuse and disuse are serious problems, often generating ineffectiveness in the home and workplace. Inappropriate or suboptimal automation usage decisions (AUDs) may also have fatal or historic consequences. Suboptimal AUDs probably contributed to the death of Casey Jones (Gurner, 2001), the surprise attack upon Pearl Harbor (Beck & Pierce, 1996), the near-meltdown at Three Mile Island (Morrissey,

1979) and the accidental sinking of a Japanese fishing boat by the USS Greenville (Savidge, 2001). Historical events sometimes pivot on the resolution of AUDs. For several weeks in November 2000, the outcome of the U.S. presidential election appeared to depend on the legal merits of automatic versus manual vote counting. The purpose of the present study is to determine if a combination of feedback and a cognitivebehavioral technique, called scenario training, effectively mitigates misuse and/or disuse.

## Automation Usage Decisions, Appraisal, and Intent Errors

Investigators have identified a number of variables that influence the likelihood that operators will rely on automation. Prominent among these are machine reliability (e.g., Dzindolet, Pierce, Beck, Dawe, & Anderson, 2001; Kantowitz, Hanowski, & Kantowitz, 1997; Metzger & Parasuraman, 2005; Parasuraman & Miller, 2004; Parasuraman & Riley, 1997; Singh, Sharma, & Parasuraman, 2001; Wiegmann, 2002; Wiegmann, Rich, & Zhang, 2001), attitudes toward automation (e.g., Halpin, Johnson, & Thornberry, 1973; Singh, Deaton, & Parasuraman, 2001; Singh, Molloy, & Parasuraman, 1993; Weil & Rosen, 1995), trust in automation (e.g., Dzindolet, Petersen, Pomranky, Pierce, & Beck, 2003; Lee & Moray, 1992; Lee & See, 2004; Moray, Inagaki, & Itoh, 2000), and feedback (e.g., Nikolic & Sarter, 2001; Singh, Hilburn, & Parasuraman,1999; Singh et al,1999; Sklar & Sarter, 1999; Wiegmann & Cristina, 2000).

Beck, Dzindolet, and Pierce (2002) proposed that AUDs often result in misuse and disuse because operators (a) are unable to determine if automation or a nonautomated alternative maximizes the likelihood of task success (appraisal errors) or (b) know the relative utilities of the options but disregard this information when deciding whether to use or not use automation (intent errors). To illustrate the difference between appraisal and intent errors, consider a soldier who receives input from a combat identification device (CID). CIDs are decision aids that soldiers use to distinguish friendly, enemy, and noncombatant forces. Assume that information from the CID is inconsistent with what the soldier perceives through the gun site and that the CID is more reliable than visual examination. Further assume that under these conditions the CID is more reliable than visual examination. An appraisal error would be committed if the soldier incorrectly concluded that visual inspection yielded the more accurate data. An intent error would occur if the soldier recognized that the CID was more likely to be correct but ignored this information and based his or her targeting decision on visual inspection.

Few investigators would question that appraisal errors frequently produce misuse and disuse. On the other hand, the proposition that operators ignore the relative utilities of the automated and nonautomated options when making AUDs is not well established. One of the objectives of this experiment is to assess intent errors in a target detection task.

The importance of understanding and mitigating errors of intent was in part suggested by a conversation with a sergeant with more than 20 years’experience. When asked about the value of CIDs, the sergeant did not discount the possibility that the U.S. Army might develop reliable target detection devices. Nevertheless, he opposed their use, contending that “when a man’s life is on the line a man and not a machine should make the decision.” It is perhaps instructive that during Operation Desert Storm a number of crews reportedly cut off certain automated devices before going into battle.

Beck et al. (2002) hypothesized that both appraisal and intent errors are sufficient to produce misuse and disuse. If that is the case, then techniques that decrease appraisal errors may have little or no effect when intent errors are prevalent. Likewise, procedures that attenuate intent errors may not reduce suboptimal decisions when operators misjudge the relative utilities of the automated and nonautomated alternatives. One implication of this analysis is that efforts to reduce suboptimal AUDs will often be more effective if they include interventions to counteract both intent and appraisal errors.

## Design and Hypotheses

A 2 (machine performance: inferior, superior) × 2 (feedback: present, absent) × 2 (scenario training: present, absent) between-subjects design was employed to test the effectiveness of feedback and scenario training. The main dependent variable was an AUD that the operator made after gaining experience with a target detection task. Student-operators were given the choice of relying on either their own performance (self-contingent credit) or that of an automated device (machine-contingent credit) referred to as a contrast detector. The outcome of this AUD affected the amount of extra credit applied to the participants’ course grades.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1. Relationship of machine performance to disuse and misuse.

AUDs were classified as optimal or suboptimal depending on the relationship of automated to operator accuracy (see Figure 1). If the detector’s accuracy exceeded that of the operator (superior machine condition), choosing machinecontingent credit was the optimal decision. Depending on one’s own performance when the detector was more accurate constituted automation disuse. If the operator outperformed the detector (inferior machine condition), electing self-contingent credit was the optimal AUD. Automation misuse would occur if the operator relied on the less accurate detector. No predictions were made regarding the relationship between the machine performance variable and the likelihood of suboptimal AUDs.

The feedback variable enabled investigators to determine whether suboptimal decisions were attributable to intent and/or appraisal errors. Although many properties of feedback influence its effectiveness (for a review see Kozlowski et al., 2001), information regarding the relative accuracies of the automated and the nonautomated options is particularly important in distinguishing intent from appraisal errors. Operators assigned to the feedback condition were told how many errors that they and the machine committed before making their AUDs. Thus, feedback prevented appraisal errors; suboptimal choices should occur in the feedback arrangements only if operators disregarded the utilities associated with self- and machine-contingent credit. Participants in the no-feedback arrangement were not told whether they were more or less accurate than the detector. Operators not given feedback needed to avoid both appraisal and intent errors in order to make optimal AUDs. That is, suboptimal decisions would result if they incorrectly estimated their accuracy relative to the detector’s accuracy (appraisal errors) and/or ignored the utilities associated with self- and machine-contingent credit (intent errors).

Fewer suboptimal AUDs were predicted in the feedback than in the no-feedback group. Support for this hypothesis would indicate that appraisal errors increased misuse and/or disuse. More importantly, a substantial number of suboptimal decisions were expected among operators receiving feedback. Such a result would show that in this experiment intent errors were an important cause of misuse and/or disuse.

Feedback may reduce appraisal errors but does little to mitigate errors of intent. Therefore, a cognitive-behavioral technique, which we termed scenario training, was developed to decrease errors of intent. Cognitive-behavioral therapies are empirically verified procedures (e.g., Heimberg & Becker, 2002; Meichenbaum & Cameron, 1974; Scaturo, 2005) that alter actions, emotions, and thought processes. Scenario training was designed to reduce intent errors by taking the operator through the thought processes of an optimal decision maker after the utilities of the automated and nonautomated alternatives had been determined. The goal of scenario training was to encourage operators to compare the utilities of the automated and nonautomated options and to subtly discourage the belief that one form of control was more “right” or appropriate than another.

For example, one scenario described a stockbroker giving investment advice. According to the passage, clients averaged a 7% return when they followed recommendations based on the broker’s personal study. Clients abiding by “advice” from a computer program showed an average gain of 4% on their investments. After reading this scenario, participants stated whether the better investment strategy was to follow recommendations founded on the stockbroker’s own study or the computer program. They were also asked to explain their reasoning. In the event of an incorrect response or “faulty” logic, the investigator furnished the “correct” choice and rationale.

To our knowledge, previous automation usage studies have not investigated the combined effects of feedback and interventions such as scenario training. If feedback attenuates appraisal errors and scenario training decreases intent errors, it is predicted that fewer suboptimal AUDs will be observed in the condition with both feedback and scenario training than in the condition with no feedback and no scenario training. Furthermore, if intent errors are a frequent cause of misuse and/or disuse, then operators assigned to the group with feedback but no scenario training will make more suboptimal AUDs than those assigned to the group with both feedback and scenario training.

## METHOD

## Participants

Undergraduates (160 women, 88 men) were recruited from a state university of approximately 13,500 students located in the southeastern United States. They were induced to volunteer by an opportunity to gain extra credit, which could be applied to their course grades. Operators were randomly assigned to conditions with the proviso that 20 women and 11 men were in each cell.

## Instrumentation

The operator’s workstation was a Hewlett-Packard Vectra, equipped with a 133-MHz central processing unit and 32 MB of RAM. Slides were presented by a S3, Inc., Trio 64 Plug-n-Play PCI video card that drove a 17-inch (43-cm) Hewlett-Packard Ultra VGA monitor set at high color (16-bit) resolution, 800 × 600 pixels. The slides were 100 color photographs taken in wooded areas at Fort Sill, Oklahoma. A compiled Visual Basic program displayed the target photographs and presented the “decisions” of the contrast detector.

The computer program was written so that the detector made approximately twice (inferior machine condition) or half as many errors (superior machine condition) as the participant did. This was accomplished by taking the accuracy of both the individual and the experimental group into account in determining how frequently the contrast detector erred. For example, if an operator assigned to the inferior machine condition committed 25 misidentifications during the session, the detector made roughly 50 errors. If a participant paired with a superior machine made 40 mistakes, the detector committed approximately 20 errors.

For programming purposes, the session was divided into 10 blocks of 20 trials each. If the operator was in the superior machine condition, the contrast detector made two errors in the first 20 trials, a performance better than that of all but a few operators. Thereafter, the detector committed half as many errors as the participants did on the preceding trial block. For example, assume an operator assigned to the superior machine condition made six errors on the fifth trial block. Three trials in the sixth trial block would then be randomly selected and the detector would be programmed to err on these trials. Because performances on the first and last trial block could not be known in advance, the ratio of detector to operator errors was not exactly 1 to 2. For a pilot group the detector $( M _ { \mathrm { p ( e r r o r ) } } = . 0 8 3 )$ to operator error $( M _ { \mathrm { p ( e r r o r ) } } = . 1 5 8 )$ ratio averaged 1.05 to 2.

If the participant worked with an inferior machine, the detector made more errors (8) on the first trial block than did the majority of operators. On the remaining trial blocks, the detector erred twice as often as the operator. If, for example, the participant made 2 errors on the fifth trial block the detector committed 4 errors on the sixth trial block. A potential problem with this procedure is that the detector could theoretically be scheduled to make more errors than there were trials. To prevent this possibility an upper limit was set so that the detector made no more than 15 errors on any 20-trial block. As a result, the detector to operator error ratio was not 2 to 1. Among pilot participants the actual machine $( M _ { \mathrm { p ( e r r o r ) } } =$.330) to operator $( M _ { \mathrm { p ( e r r o r ) } }   =   . 1 7 6 )$ error ratio averaged 1.88 to 1.

## Procedure

Scenario training and the control condition. Before beginning the target detection task, half of the participants received scenario training. Operators given scenario training were presented with four situations in which an individual chose between automated and nonautomated alternatives. In addition to the stockbroker passage, the scenarios involved a pilot, a store manager, and a quiz show contestant. Automation was the optimal AUD in two of the scenarios, and the non-automated alternative was the optimal choice in the other two scenarios. Participants who did not receive scenario training served as a control condition. They read and answered questions from a short article summarizing the history of automation. This material was designed to appear to be related to other aspects of the study but furnished no information that would assist in performing the experimental task or in making AUDs.

Training trials. Training trials were conducted after participants received the scenarios or responded to the history of automation passage. A target detection task, similar to one employed in several other investigations (Dzindolet, Pierce, Beck, & Dawe, 2002; Dzindolet et al., 2001) of misuse and disuse, was employed. The purposes of the training trials were to give operators experience with the experimental task and the opportunity to compare their accuracy with that of the contrast detector. Operators worked individually in a room containing the workstation, a table, and chairs. Participants were informed that they would view a series of slides on the computer screen, half of which contained a male soldier in camouflage. They were instructed that their task was to determine whether or not the soldier was present in each slide. Operators were told that two types of errors were possible, both of which were equally serious. One form of error was deciding that the soldier was present when he was not. The second type of error was concluding that the soldier was absent when he was in the photograph.

Trials began with the display of a photograph on the monitor for 0.75 s. A screen then appeared asking if the soldier was in the preceding slide. Responses were made via mouse by clicking a “button” on the screen. Following the participant’s decision, a computer routine supposedly searched “for contrasts that suggest the presence of a human being.” The results of the scan were then shown in the “contrast detector box.” The word “Present” appeared alongside a red circle in the box if the routine concluded that a soldier was in the photograph. If the scan found no evidence of a human form, the word “Absent” and a green circle were shown in the box. Operators were advised that the automated device was “not perfect” and that they were not necessarily wrong if they disagreed with the contrast detector.

Next, four practice trials were performed during which students were encouraged to pose questions. They were then asked to describe the task. When the experimenter was confident that the participants understood the instructions, he or she left the room. Each photograph was presented twice for a total of 200 trials.

After the last training trial, a screen requested that the participant ask the experimenter to return to the room containing the workstation. Students in the feedback conditions then clicked a button to reveal a screen showing that the contrast detector made twice or half as many errors as they did over the preceding trials. No participants indicated that they were aware that the detector’s accuracy was geared to their own performance or that the exact ratio of detector to operator errors was not 2 to 1 (inferior machine condition) or 1 to 2 (superior machine condition). The number of errors made by the operator and detector were displayed until the participant clicked a button to advance to the next screen. Operators who were not assigned to the feedback condition were not told how many errors they and the machine committed.

Credit trials. The experimenter then informed the students that the opportunity to earn extra credit had arrived. Participants were instructed that 10 “credit trials” would be randomly selected from the 200 training trials that they and the contrast detector had just completed. Operators were told that outcomes of the credit trials would then be “reviewed” and that the points they received for serving in the experiment depended entirely how many of the 10 trials were answered correctly. Participants were given the option of basing their extra credit points on their own performance or on the performance of the contrast detector. If students opted for self-contingent credit, only their responses to the credit trials determined the points that they gained. If they chose machine-contingent credit, their points solely depended on how many of the credit trials the detector answered correctly.

Students summarized these instructions for the experimenter and then clicked a button indicating whether their points were to be contingent on their decisions or the detector’s decisions. Before the credit trials were conducted, operators provided written explanations describing why they chose to base credit on their own or the detector’s responses. Prior to receiving these directions they were not aware that they would be requested to furnish rationales. After the participants completed their written descriptions, the credit trials were performed. If the operators elected self-contingent credit, the screen displayed the operator’s response to each credit trial, whether or not a soldier was present on that trial, and the total points the student received. Operators choosing machine-contingent credit were shown the same information except that the detector’s rather than the participant’s responses were displayed. Operators were then thanked and debriefed.

## RESULTS

## Analysis of Automation Usage Decisions

AUDs were defined as suboptimal if an operator paired with an inferior machine based extra credit on the contrast detector or if an operator paired with a superior machine elected self-contingent credit. The initial plan was to conduct a 2 (machine performance: inferior, superior) × 2 (feedback: present, absent) × 2 (scenario training: present, absent) ANOVAusing suboptimal AUDs as the dependent measure (see Table 1). Because the misuse rate was very low (total suboptimal decisions = 3, 2%), no statistical analyses were performed upon the AUDs of operators paired with an inferior machine.

In contrast to the low misuse rate, the overall disuse rate (total suboptimal decisions = 79) was 64%. A2 (feedback: present, absent) × 2 (scenario training: present, absent)between-subjects ANOVA was performed upon the choices of participants assigned to the superior machine condition. The main effect for feedback was statistically significant main, $F(1,120)=36.19,p<.001$ , partial eta squared = .23. As predicted, in the superior machine condition, operators who received feedback made fewer suboptimal AUDs than operators assigned to the no-feedback group. The main effect for scenario training did not attain statistical significance, F(1, 120) = 1.62, p > .05, partial eta squared = .01. However, the Feedback × Scenario Training interaction was statistically significant, F(1, 120) = 4.62, $p < . 0 5$ , partial eta squared = .04.

A series of Tukey b post hoc comparisons were made between groups of operators who were teamed with a superior machine. Feedback without scenario training produced a statistically significant decrease in the disuse rate. Of the participants without scenario training, those who received feedback made significantly fewer suboptimal choices (55%) than did those assigned to the no-feedback group (84%), $p < . 0 5$ . Scenario training did not affect the incidence of suboptimal choices if operators did not receive feedback following the 200th trial. In the no-feedback groups, no statistical difference was observed in the frequencies of suboptimal AUDs between those who received scenario training (87%) and those who did not (84%), $p > . 0 5$ . When coupled with feedback, scenario training attenuated the incidence of disuse. With feedback, students in the scenario training condition (29%) made significantly fewer suboptimal AUDs than students in the condition with no scenario training (55%), $p <$.05. The prediction that a combination of feedback and scenario training would reduce suboptimal AUDs was also supported. Suboptimal choices were less common among those given both feedback and scenario training (29%) than those given neither feedback nor scenario training (84%), $p < . 0 5$

## Analysis of Operators’ Explanations for Their AUDs

Before operators’ rationales for choosing self-versus machine-contingent credit could be assessed, it was first necessary to develop a system for categorizing attributions. A research assistant began this process by typing the operators’ handwritten rationales onto a computer file. Transcriptions were verbatim except that grammatical errors and misspellings were corrected. Each attribution was labeled so that it could later be identified with a particular operator.

Labels were then removed, and the first author of this article was furnished a randomized list of the operators’explanations. From these statements, five types of attributions were defined: perceived utility (operator compared the outcomes of automated and nonautomated options over many trials), availability (AUD was based on the results of one or a few easily recalled trials), responsibility/control (rationale indicated a desire to assume or to avoid personal accountability for the performance or outcome of the AUD), satisficing (operator employed the first alternative whose expected outcome was deemed satisfactory), and miscellaneous.

Three undergraduate assistants, who were not otherwise involved in the experiment, were trained to code the operators’attributions. Coders worked independently, reading each rationale and assigning it to one or more categories. A rationale was recorded as reflecting a particular category if two or more assistants so judged. Among operators paired with a superior machine, those reporting that their decisions were based on perceived utility tended to make optimal choices, $\chi ^ { 2 } ( 1 )   =   3 9 . 0 8$ $p < .001, \phi^{2} = .31$ . Participants whose rationales indicated satisficing, $\chi^{2}(1)=6.44, p<.05, \phi^{2}=$.05, availability, $\chi^{2}(1)=17.66,p<.001,\phi^{2}=.14,$ , and responsibility/control, $\chi^{2}(1)=11.99,p<.001,\phi^{2}=$.10, tended to make suboptimal AUDS.

## DISCUSSION

Because disuse was more frequent than misuse, the impact of feedback and scenario training was greatest among participants working alongside a superior machine. Of the 31 participants assigned to the condition with a superior machine, no feedback, and no scenario training, 26 made suboptimal decisions, a baseline disuse rate of 84%. This outcome is the laboratory analogue of employees refusing to use potentially helpful automation in the workplace. Although the data demonstrate the effectiveness of feedback, they also indicate the resistance of intent errors to disconfirming information. Over half (55%) of the participants in the condition with a superior machine and feedback but no scenario training based extra credit on their own rather than the machine’s performance. Feedback was more successful in decreasing disuse when it was combined with scenario training, an intervention developed to combat intent errors. When used in tandem, 29% of the operators in the condition with a superior machine, feedback, and scenario training made suboptimal choices, almost a two-thirds reduction below baseline. Extrapolation of these results suggests that operator training programs should incorporate techniques to control the occurrence of intent as well as appraisal errors.

Perceived utility was associated with optimal decisions, whereas satisficing, availability, and responsibility/control attributions were associated with suboptimal AUDs. Although the data do not conclusively indicate why feedback and scenario training were effective, the participants’rationales suggest that these interventions prompted operators to compare self- and machine-contingent credit and then to choose the alternative that was likely to yield the most points. A further perusal of the rationales suggests that rivalry may have influenced the AUDs of some operators assigned to the groups with a superior machine and feedback. Not surprisingly, most participants electing machine-contingent credit reported that they valued the detector as a tool for increasing their points. In contrast, many of the operators choosing self-contingent credit saw the machine as a competitor. It is reasonable to surmise that future investigations will find that intent errors, like appraisal errors, have multiple determinants. It also seems likely that many of these studies will discover that perceptions of rivalry often lead operators to disregard the utilities of automated and nonautomated alternatives when making AUDs.

Additional studies need to assess the influence of other factors on the probability of appraisal and intent errors and the interventions employed to control them. The type of task, the personality and attitudes of the operator, the magnitude of task consequences, and the number of automation levels to choose from are some of the variables that probably affect the generalization of the current findings. Certainly, one of the most critical questions arising from these data is whether professionally trained operators are susceptible to intent errors.

Without discounting the possibility that intent errors are restricted to untrained operators, it may be overly optimistic to assume that persons charged with great responsibilities do not sometimes perceive machines as rivals or ignore information indicating that automation would increase the likelihood of a successful task performance. The social and cognitive literatures are replete with variables that could lead professional operators to disregard the utilities associated with automated and nonautomated alternatives. For example, dislike for automation in general could set the stage for intent errors. Operators may also base their AUDs on the belief that it is either ethical or unethical to automate certain tasks. A need to “take control” (Langer & Roth, 1975; Rodin & Langer, 1980; Taylor, 1989; Thompson, 1981) or boredom could also cause operators to reject high levels of automation.

The results of this investigation, anecdotal evidence, and findings from related research areas do not necessarily mean that professional operators are susceptible to intent errors. They do, however, demonstrate the need to study intent errors among trained operators in more realistic settings. To a great extent, acceptance and efficient use of new technologies by professional and nonprofessional operators will depend upon the ability to control intent and appraisal errors. Advances in the reliability of decision aids and other automated devices will be a hollow achievement unless the current knowledge of hardware and software is matched by an equally sophisticated comprehension of the causes and control of misuse and disuse.
